guides.title: About this website
guides.subtitle: How to use these Easy Read guides

lines: A pharmacist in Adelaide made this guide.
When you see the word **we**, it means the pharmacist who runs this website.
We wrote this information in an easy to read way.
We use pictures to explain some ideas.
We wrote some important words in **bold**.
This means the letters are thicker and darker.
We explain what these words mean in the word list at the end.
This is an Easy Read summary of our website.
It only has the most important ideas.
The full website is at **www.gamsa.au**
You can ask for help to read this guide.
A friend, family member, support person or your pharmacist may be able to help you.
Some trans and gender diverse people take **hormone medicines**.
These medicines change your body over time.
Doctors call this **gender-affirming hormone therapy**.
People often have questions about these medicines, like:
- how much they cost
- what to do when a chemist has none left
- how to use them safely.
The answers are usually written for doctors and pharmacists.
They can be hard to find and hard to read.
We made this guide to help.
This guide does not tell you what medicine to take.
Your doctor or nurse decides that with you.
There is one Easy Read guide for each thing you might need to do.
You can read them in any order.
Each one can be printed or saved as a PDF.

guides.title: Getting your medicine
guides.subtitle: Prescriptions, the pharmacy and your name on the label

lines: First you see a doctor or a nurse who can prescribe.
If they agree the medicine is right for you, they write a **prescription**.
A prescription is a note that lets you get the medicine.
Then you take the prescription to a pharmacy.
A pharmacy is also called a chemist.
It helps to use the same pharmacy each time.
The staff get to know you.
They can order your medicine in before you run out.
Your medicine label might show a name you do not use.
This is because the pharmacy computer uses your Medicare name.
You can ask the pharmacy to put your **preferred name** on the label.
Your preferred name is the name you want people to use.
Some staff will not know how to do this straight away.
They may need to ring the people who make their computer program.
It is okay to ask them to find out.

sections.h: If you live far from the city

lines: Country pharmacies keep less medicine on the shelf.
Ask for your medicine a week before you run out.
An **e-script** is a prescription on your phone.
You can send it to any pharmacy in Australia.
Some pharmacies will post your medicine to you.
Your doctor can see you by phone or video. This is called **telehealth**.
If you must travel a long way to see a specialist, you may get help with the cost.
In South Australia this help is called **PATS**.

guides.title: When a medicine is hard to get
guides.subtitle: Shortages and what to do

sections.h: When a medicine is hard to get

lines: Some days a medicine runs out across the whole country.
This is called a **shortage**.
It is not your fault and it is not your pharmacy's fault.
Our website checks the official shortage list every day.
It shows which hormone medicines are hard to get right now.
If your medicine is hard to get:
- talk to your pharmacist early
- do not wait until you have run out
- ask them to order some in for you.
Your pharmacist may be able to give you a different **brand**.
A different brand is the same medicine in a different box.
This is safe and normal.

guides.title: Paying for your medicine
guides.subtitle: The PBS, concession cards and Closing the Gap

lines: The government pays for most of the cost of many medicines.
This is called the **PBS**.
You pay the rest. This part is called a **co-payment**.
Most people pay up to **$25.00** for a PBS medicine.
If you have a concession card, you pay up to **$7.70**.
If you buy a lot of medicine in one year, the cost goes down.
This is called the **Safety Net**.
Ask your pharmacy to keep a record for you.
Some medicines are not on the PBS.
These cost more.
The website has a page that explains each one.
If the cost is too much, tell your pharmacist.
They can often help.
You are not the first person to ask.
**Closing the Gap** is a government plan.
It aims to make health fairer for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
Part of it makes medicines cheaper.
If you are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, ask your doctor to sign you up.
You only need to do this once.
After that, PBS medicines cost less at any pharmacy.
If you have a concession card, they are free.

guides.title: Using patches and gel
guides.subtitle: Medicine that goes on your skin

lines: A **patch** is a small sticker with medicine inside.
It goes on clean, dry skin.
The medicine goes through your skin slowly.
Most patches are changed twice a week.
Pick the same two days every week.
Put each new patch on a different spot.
Do not put a patch on your chest or breast.
Do not put it where a belt or waistband rubs.
If a patch falls off, put on a new one.
**Gel** is medicine you rub on your skin, usually once a day.
Put it where the box says. Let it dry before you get dressed.
Wash your hands straight after.
Keep other people and pets away from the gel.
Wait until your skin is dry and covered.
This matters most for children and pregnant people.
Ask your pharmacist to show you. You can ask to talk somewhere private.

guides.title: Having an injection
guides.subtitle: What happens, and what to tell your nurse or doctor

lines: Some hormone medicines are given as an **injection**.
Some you have every few weeks. Some you have every few months.
Tell the nurse or doctor if you feel unwell.
Also tell them if an injection has made you sick before.
The long-acting testosterone injection is given slowly, into the side of your hip.
You then wait in the clinic for about 15 minutes.
This is normal. It is so staff can help if you have a rare reaction.
Tell staff straight away if you:
- cough a lot
- feel short of breath
- feel dizzy
- have chest pain.
After you leave, ring 000 if any of these happen.
Ask when your next injection is due before you leave.
Write it down.
Some people learn to give their own injections.
Only do this after a nurse or doctor has taught you.
Practise with them first.
Never share needles.
Put used needles in a sharps bin, not in the rubbish.
Your pharmacy can tell you where to get a sharps bin.

guides.title: Taking tablets and capsules
guides.subtitle: Swallowing your medicine the right way

lines: Take your tablets the way your doctor told you.
Take them at about the same time each day.
Some tablets go under your tongue instead of being swallowed. The label will say.
If you are not sure, ask your pharmacist.
If you forget a dose, take it when you remember.
If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one.
Never take two doses at once to catch up.
Keep tablets in their box, somewhere cool and dry, away from children.

guides.title: Understanding your dose
guides.subtitle: What the numbers on your medicine mean

lines: A **dose** is how much medicine you take, and how often.
It is written on your medicine label.
The numbers are in **milligrams (mg)** or **micrograms (mcg)**.
A microgram is a thousand times smaller than a milligram.
That is why patches say 50 mcg and tablets say 2 mg. They are different medicines in different amounts.

sections.h: Why doses are different for different people

lines: Everyone is different.
Your doctor works out your dose from your blood tests and how you feel.
Someone else's dose is not your dose.
Many people start on a low dose.
The dose often goes up slowly over months.
Do not change your dose on your own.
Taking more does not make changes happen faster, and it can be unsafe.
You will have **blood tests** from time to time. They show your doctor if the dose is right.
If you want your dose changed, talk to your doctor.
That is a normal thing to ask.

guides.title: Where to get help
guides.subtitle: People who can help, and a word list

lines: Take your medicine the way your doctor told you.
Take it at about the same time each day.
Some medicines are patches or gels that go on your skin.
Some are tablets you swallow.
Some are injections.
If you are not sure how to use your medicine, ask your pharmacist.
You can ask to talk somewhere private.
If you feel unwell after taking your medicine, get help.
Ring your doctor.
In an emergency, ring **000**.
If English is not your first language, you can get a free **interpreter**.
Ring **TIS National** on **131 450**.
Ask them to call your doctor or pharmacy for you.
The full website is at **www.gamsa.au**
It has a page for each medicine.
You can ring **healthdirect** on **1800 022 222** to talk to a nurse.
This is free and open all day and all night.
You can tell us if something on the website is wrong or missing.
We want to fix it.
